# Applications: Lessons in Chemistry: Impact of Teammate Familiarity on Shooting in the NBA

## Where this applies

- Inference: Early-season reading of PFF and efficiency numbers for new pairings (a transfer quarterback with new receivers, or an offensive line with new combinations). The talk's claim is that a pair's results improve quickly over its first attempts together [09:43]. Decision: how much weight to give a new pairing's September numbers when grading or adjusting plans.
- Inference: Keep a simple counter of shared reps for chosen starter pairs in camp and practice, using existing film tags or GPS session logs. The talk's model used two counters, one in-season and one cumulative across seasons [08:40].
- Inference: Return-to-performance reintegration. When a starter returns to a unit, log how results change in the first weeks back. The speakers said their model has no notion of breaks and that decay after a layoff is an open question [33:19], [33:49]. Treat this as a hypothesis to log, not a rule.
- Inference: Before crediting a training or testing change, establish the normal curve for the same group. A speaker said the starting point for studying any intervention is the normal expected curve [30:15].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: new movement patterns take roughly 3 to 4 weeks of practice to become efficient (course material, speaker unconfirmed, so a course team position, Inferred). The talk agrees in direction (a steep early gain, then slow gain) and extends it to pairs of players rather than one athlete. The talk measures shots, not weeks, so the two time scales are not directly comparable.
- Eric's baseline: weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent testing to catch plateaus early, and testing protocols must be exactly repeatable (course material, Inferred). The talk agrees: its result depends on counting every attempt the same way.
- Eric's baseline: preparedness (built over a long period) is distinguished from readiness (day to day) (course material, Inferred). The talk's carry-over between seasons [10:14] is an example of the slow component for a pair, but the talk does not use these terms.

## What would have to be true

- Shared reps or targets for a pair can be counted reliably (film tags, consistent grading) and there are enough of them to see a curve. The NBA data had up to 237 catch-and-shoot attempts for the most frequent pair and rarely more than 200 in a season [07:38], [09:43].
- A shot-quality-style baseline exists for the football play type chosen, so that selection and execution can be separated. The talk split gains about half into shot quality and half into accuracy [15:54], [16:26].
- The pairing changed because of a roster move, not because of injury or benching, so the comparison is fair.

## Do not apply when

- The play type is rare or has few attempts per pair. Football pass plays per quarterback-receiver pair are far fewer than repeated catch-and-shoot attempts in basketball (Inference), and the speakers said individual pair curves are noisy and biased [21:33].
- Used to rank individual players or pairs. The speakers said slicing by player or pair adds insight and also adds noise [25:38].
- The effect is presented as proven cause. It is an average learning curve with a simple model, and the speakers described their numbers as rule of thumb [17:27].
- The setting is pro salary and trade decisions. A speaker said trading for pairs is not advised and that trading money for talent is a bigger effect [39:02], [39:32].

## First step

Choose one unit (for example quarterback and top three receivers). List the new pairings this season and tally shared practice reps from existing film tags for two weeks. Record only. Make no decision changes until there are enough reps to look at.

# Applications: Causal Impact of Offensive Linemen on Pass Plays

## Where this applies

- Inference: Reading vendor player grades (PFF and similar) with a fixed question list: what does the number condition on, who else influenced the play, and is it a residual from a prediction model? The speaker contrasted residual-style metrics (his example was rush yards over expected) with a method aimed at cause and effect [00:30], [02:00]. Decision: which vendor metrics go into recruiting and transfer grading for offensive linemen and which stay as film notes.
- Inference: Offensive line film review. Take plays where a lineman was charged with allowing pressure and the pass was still completed (or the reverse), and check film for where credit was misassigned. The talk showed per-lineman credit changing tenth by tenth of a second on one play [04:31], [05:01].
- Inference: Apply the same causal framing to an athlete-monitoring question, for example whether a high-speed-running exposure leads to a lower force plate mRSI the next day once position and practice plan are accounted for. The speaker only claimed the framework extends to other positions and sports [09:05], [09:35]. The monitoring use is my own extension and untested.
- Inference: When a college tracking source is available, ask the vendor how the model adjusts for competition level, since the speaker said that matters more in college than in the NFL [12:35].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Eric-authored SportSmith). The talk shows a high-cost, high-complexity method. The baseline suggests asking whether the extra insight beats simpler metrics for a given decision. The talk does not compare costs.
- Eric's baseline: metric selection for force plates follows Output, Driver and Strategy groupings (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics, not Eric's own framework). The talk's completion outcome and its pressure driver echo that structure, but the talk does not use those terms. No direct link found for football tracking beyond this.

## What would have to be true

- Play-level x,y tracking for Baylor's and opponents' games, at consistent quality (the speaker said computer vision tracking exists at the college level [12:35]).
- A consistent, non-subjective definition of pressure allowed.
- Enough pass plays per lineman for a stable estimate. The talk did not report play counts.
- Validation that goes beyond honors and salary. The talk validated against All-Pro and Pro Bowl honors, salary ranking and PFF [06:33], [07:03].

## Do not apply when

- The data are not tracking data. A grade alone cannot support this method.
- The only evidence is the talk. The speaker works at Sumer Sports and described the method as theirs (commercial view), and the public sample was the first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season [07:03].
- Decisions about one lineman rest on the number alone. Validation against reputation and salary shows agreement with consensus, not proof of cause (Inference).
- The pass-play credit share is read literally. The talk gave 10 to 15% attributed to the line on one play and 60 to 80% on another, and did not explain the gap [05:01], [06:01].

## First step

Pull 20 pass plays with a low PFF pass-block grade and a completion, plus 20 with a high grade and pressure allowed. Review film with the offensive line staff and count where the grade looks misassigned. One hour of review, no change to grading practice.

One executive described a probability distribution from base rates for players of a given type, then downside, middle and upside outcomes, expected value and variance [16:59]. Another spoke of the 90th and 10th percentile outcomes [21:03]. Decision: each new evaluation states a low, middle and high expected outcome and the reasons.
- Inference: A fixed pre-check before acting on a player who suddenly becomes available (portal or release). The Texans executive described a database grade, scout view, coach view of role fit, then a call [25:39], [26:10]. A Baylor version adds an Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance lane (testing history, availability), as an input and not a decision.
- Inference: Review decisions by process as well as outcome. A panelist said judging a transaction only on near-term results is a way to "drive ourselves crazy" [18:31], and another said to learn from wins that were played poorly [33:55]. Decision: after the season, review why a test, a tool or a monitoring practice was kept or dropped, separately from what happened after.
- Inference: Plan depth for soft-tissue injuries by position instead of waiting for a risk model. The baseball executive said that until the field improves injury rates, the team builds as much depth as possible [37:32].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: the NordBord decision rule. Keep a demanding test only with "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" and drop it where consistent collection cannot be guaranteed (Eric-authored SportSmith). The panel's process-over-outcome point agrees: the baseline judges the decision by its conditions, not by one result.
- Eric's baseline: injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (course material, Inferred, and a gap noted in the baseline). The baseball depth remark agrees with the first half. It does not supply a model.
- Eric's baseline: recruiting grading is not covered in the method baseline. No direct link found for the first two uses above.

## What would have to be true

- There is a consistent recruiting or portal grading form so ranges can be compared across evaluations.
- Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance agree on what they will share, and in which format, before a player decision.
- Enough past evaluations exist to state base rates for a player type. The talk shows no data for this.

## Do not apply when

- Pro contract and payroll logic does not transfer. Price per win, salary cap rules and trade chart arguments [14:54], [21:33] are pro mechanics, and college roster, transfer and NIL rules differ.
- The stories are taken as typical. A panelist said executives tend to pick the good stories [11:52].
- The panelists' own pay and results are the justification. Their views are institutional and this is a conversation with no data shown.
- Draft-day reasoning is used to guide athlete monitoring. The panel did not discuss monitoring.

## First step

Take the last two recruit or portal evaluations. Write a low, middle and high expected outcome for each with one sentence of reasons, file it, and revisit after the season. No change to the live grading form.

=== FILE: videos/2025-03-18_MyfHUiOnsSY_the-analytics-driven-franchise-building-a-modern-nba-team/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: MyfHUiOnsSY
title: "SSAC25: The Analytics Driven Franchise: Building a Modern NBA Team"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ariana andan (caption spelling), Shane Bader (caption spelling), Monty McNair, Oliver (caption spelling; data scientist at ESPN), John Hollinger (moderator)]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, sports-science, injury-health, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A panel of four NBA figures and a moderator on how teams turn a growing flood of data (tracking, new pose data, sports science) into decisions. The panelists argue the raw data advantage has largely standardized, so the edge now lies in analysis and, most of all, in throughput: getting a few high-leverage points to front office, coaches and players in a form each can use. They cover limits of predictive models, injuries and workload as the area with the most room to grow, the psychology of sharing numbers with players, and the need to combine analytics with the eye test. Evidence is anecdotal and no data are shown.

## Key claims

- Analytics departments have grown. The question is where information gets throughput, so a team has to pick the highest-leverage information that can affect winning. [01:30]
- Tracking data has been available for roughly ten years and pose data is new, so teams are "behind again." Sports science also offers more information than teams know what to do with. [02:00]
- Pose data will be something teams chase for the next 5 to 10 years. [02:31]
- Players can be overloaded with information. Instincts should be built in practice, and some players tell staff they have had enough. [03:02]
- The decisions (who to play, how to improve) are the same as 20 or 40 years ago. Numbers refine them, and staff should filter before information reaches users. [03:34]
- A player on the panel accepted "the answers to the test" and said clear communication of the value to the player drives receptiveness. [04:04], [04:34]
- Staff take information to coaches, coaches pick what reaches players, and the format varies by player (a booklet for one, three clips for another). [05:04], [05:35]
- Players in their 30s grew up in the analytics generation and may be more comfortable with it than some coaches. [06:06]
- A data advantage is largely going away because the league has standardized it. Two other layers remain: how well you analyze it, and throughput into decisions and onto the floor. Getting data into the organization's mindset is called the final frontier. [08:09], [08:40], [09:11]
- The same data can support opposing arguments about one player. [09:11], [09:42]
- Analytics to coaching and medical work is more indirect than acquisition: numbers suggest a treatment, reach the trainer, then reach the player through a relationship. [09:42], [10:12]
- For prediction, the best model might move an All-Star chance from 60% to 68%, which is not dramatic for one player but adds up across many. A panelist thinks draft models have not improved much in 15 years. Player development also matters to whether a player lands in the 68% or the 32%. [11:13], [11:44]
- A scouting-side panelist sees improvement over about 10 years, mostly in how models are used alongside the eye test, and finds accuracy hard to judge. [12:16], [12:46]
- Injury prevention is where there is the most room to grow. The game is faster, players play over the summer, and interpreting a number needs a partnership with the player about how they feel. [13:47], [14:17]
- Teams have become more conservative because they want players healthy for long periods. Players arrive with more miles and the implications are not known. [15:18], [15:49]
- A panelist said there is evidence that players learn more between seasons than during them. Sleep has improved (no 9 a.m. practice after a late arrival, a nap culture). [16:20]
- The remaining barrier is communication. Data staff should add communication skills and non-quantitative staff should learn the language, so both meet in the middle. [17:51], [18:22], [18:52]
- Basketball value is contextual (a named Memphis pair fit the team's style). Teams should find similar past situations and merge the evaluation system with scouts and coaches. [19:53], [20:24]
- Comparing international leagues to the NBA has not been solved. [20:54], [21:25]
- A player on the panel did not want to know his weaknesses. A 2009 article about a "no stats All-Star" was followed by about two months of that player shooting less. [22:25], [22:56]
- Staff should decide what to tell a player, when, how and why. One panelist showed a star his free throw footage from four years earlier instead of numbers, and it helped. [23:58], [24:29], [25:29]
- Irrational confidence is important at this level. [25:29], [26:01]
- Next frontiers named: sports science and player performance, new pose data, reading body language and facial expressions. [26:31], [27:01], [27:31]
- Handling pressure in a game is the skill that separates Hall of Famers, and mental potential is called the Holy Grail. [28:01], [28:33]
- Subjective inputs (intel scores, coach ratings) can go into models if they have a consistent history, but the history is harder to collect, and psychological assessment is not standardized across NBA teams. [29:36], [30:07]
- A panelist called the NBA the most efficient draft of the major leagues. Mixed lineups allow a top-down view of whether a team wins when a player is on the floor, though it can take a lot of time to show. [31:08], [32:10]
- The new collective bargaining agreement has not slowed trades. Teams use third or fourth teams to complete deals, and cap staff teach the rest of the front office. [32:40], [33:11], [35:47]
- Audience Q&A: the next-generation executive needs breadth, humility and communication, and luck matters. A coach-story line was "if you do not have good players you will not win." [34:13], [34:44]

## Numbers and definitions

- First conference was 19 years ago, per the moderator. [00:30]
- Tracking data: "eight nine years whatever it is 10 years." [02:00]
- 82 games in 177 days ("or whatever it is"). [02:31]
- All-Star probability example: 60% to 68%, and the 32% complement. [11:13], [11:44]
- Draft models not much better "in the last 15 years" (panelist's view). [11:13]
- Westbrook free throw example: over 80% for eight or nine years, then "60 something." [24:59]
- A 90% win probability graph example: a three-point lead with a minute to go. [38:51]
- A draft has "60 players or 59 or 58." [30:07]
- Panel runs 40 minutes plus 5 for questions. [00:30]
- Garble risk: the panelist names in the introduction are caption-misspelled and no captions label which panelist is speaking.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Three layers of edge: data, analysis, throughput. [08:09], [08:40]
- Staff-to-coach-to-player communication chain, with information tailored to the player. [05:04]
- Merging an evaluation system with scouts and coaches, and looking for similar past fits. [20:24]
- Distilling subjective scouting or coaching ratings into consistent scores that can be tested for predictiveness. [29:36]
- Using eye test and analytics separately to find and explain disagreements. [45:04], [45:34]

## Limits and open questions

- Panel conversation with no data shown, no sample sizes, and claims are mostly anecdote.
- Captions carry no speaker labels, so most claims cannot be assigned to a named panelist.
- Unnamed sources: "there is evidence" on learning between seasons, and "all the research" on sleep [16:20].
- Organizational views (team culture, front-office staffing) are the panelists' own institutional positions.
- A panelist said data advantage is fading [08:09] while another said teams are "behind again" on new data [02:00]. Both can hold, but the panel does not reconcile them.
- The LeBron and Durant story rests on two possessions, and the speaker said he did not raise sample size and variance [42:59], [43:30].

## Q&A

- Next-generation executives: luck, humility, breadth, communication. [34:13]
- Are recent coach-players more receptive to analytics? Yes, more open, with a minimal working level that is higher than before. [37:19]
- Negative effects of analytics: fans find the game too complicated, and a misleading win probability graph. [38:20], [38:51]
- Analytics in officiating: positive if it creates a meritocracy, with a guard against people changing behavior to fit the measure. [39:53], [40:25]
- Value of generational leaders: spacing, turnover saving and shot selection that filters down, plus tone. [41:56]
- Analytics versus the eye test: use both, and examine disagreements. [44:33], [45:34]

=== FILE: videos/2025-03-18_o4rMbhsdk0I_lessons-in-chemistry-impact-of-teammate-familiarity-on-shoot/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: o4rMbhsdk0I
title: "SSAC25: Lessons in Chemistry: Impact of Teammate Familiarity on Shooting in the NBA"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Alamar, Dean Oliver]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Alamar and Dean Oliver study whether NBA teammates shoot better the more they play together. They build a shot-quality model from NBA tracking and pressure data, then regress shot quality and accuracy on counters of how many catch-and-shoot attempts a passer and shooter have had together. They report a steep early gain over the first 50 attempts, slower gain to about 200, partial carry-over into the next season, and roughly half the gain from better shot selection and half from accuracy. The speakers call the numbers rule of thumb and stress noise. Most of the talk is a long audience Q&A raising possible extensions.

## Key claims

- After acquiring Chris Paul, Phoenix started slowly, then finished the season strongly; points per attempt on shots off his passes started well below league average and improved. [02:00], [02:31]
- Kyrie Irving and Russell Westbrook are cited as similar anecdotal cases, which motivated a systematic look. [03:31], [04:02], [04:34]
- The study ignores turnovers (harder to study) and looks at shots. [05:04]
- Shot quality improves as passer-shooter pairs play together. Shorter two-point shots, lower pressure on the passer, and more open shots (about 4% lower pressure score in the first 100 shots) are the measurable drivers. [10:47], [11:18], [11:48]
- Accuracy above expected also improves, with a curve of similar shape. [12:18], [12:49]
- The speaker (a former coach) offers confidence, rhythm and timing, and pass placement preferences as unmodeled reasons for accuracy gains. These are the speaker's explanations, not tested. [13:52], [14:22], [15:23]
- About half the gain comes from shot quality and half from accuracy. [15:54], [16:26]
- Gains are largest early, with diminishing marginal gains across seasons, and the data set does not hold enough long-tenured pairs to find a maximum. Two to three seasons together are beneficial. [19:31], [20:01]
- Practice data would be the prescriptive side, and teams hold it. [20:32], [21:03]
- Team-level integration effects and plug-and-play players are named as open, and individual pair results are noisy and biased. [21:33], [22:04]
- Positional analysis (big to big passing) was not done. [22:34]
- Results are stronger for catch-and-shoot than for all shot types. [24:07]
- Chemistry here means familiarity in catch-and-shoot situations only. Lineup-level work needs care because good lineups play more together. [30:45], [31:16]
- A speaker says to study learning, first establish the normal expected curve, then see whether an intervention improves it. [30:15]
- The model has no notion of a break within a season, so decay after injury is untested. [33:19], [33:49]
- Turnover and incompletion reasons are not categorized in basketball as they are in football. [36:56], [37:28]
- An interaction between season and attempt count was statistically significant but did not change the shape much. [37:59], [38:30]
- Asked about trading for pairs of players, a speaker said no, and that trading money for talent is a bigger effect. [39:02], [39:32]

## Numbers and definitions

- Data: 1600 passer-shooter combinations with between 10 and 50 catch-and-shoot attempts, averaging 1.12 points per attempt, 2023-24 season. [07:38]
- Most frequent pair: 237 catch-and-shoot attempts (captions: "Tyrese and Miles"). [07:38]
- Expected points = made-shot probability times 2 or 3. [07:08]
- Shot probability inputs: shot type, location, and NBA-supplied pressure scores (passer pressure, receiver pressure, shooter pressure, defined by defender closeness). [06:06], [06:37]
- Models tried: XGBoost (best), random forest (weird results), logistic regression (not as good). [06:37], [07:08]
- Familiarity model: a simple log-log regression with an in-season counter and a cumulative counter of passer-shooter catch-and-shoot attempts. [08:40], [09:13]
- Result: about 7% improvement in the first 50 attempts, another 4% to 200. Rarely more than 200 attempts in a season. [09:43]
- Carry-over: next season starts about 5% above where the pair started in season one, below the end of season one. [10:14]
- Accuracy analysis assumes a 1.2 expected-points baseline. [12:18]
- Phoenix trio: from 81 points per 100 shots to 93, then more up to about 200 shots (rule of thumb). [17:27]
- Garble risk: "started off I believe it was 11 and N" and "about 40 and 20 something" [02:00], "8 low well below" [02:31], and "a 7% field goal percentage" [16:26] are garbled, and the units of the 7% and 4% gains are not stated clearly.

## Methods and frameworks named

- NBA-provided tracking and pressure data; a custom shot-quality model with gradient boosting.
- Log-log regression of shot quality and of actual minus expected points on two counters of shared attempts. [08:40]
- Decomposition of the gain into shot quality and accuracy. [15:54]

## Limits and open questions

- The speakers described the model as a first step and the numbers as rule of thumb [17:27]. They did not show controls for selection into shared playing time (shown only for lineups as a caution [31:16]).
- The explanations for accuracy are the speaker's coaching view and are not in the model. [13:52]
- Pair-level results are noisy and biased. [21:33]
- No positional, rookie-specific, break-decay, shot-frequency or role-player analysis. [22:34], [33:49], [34:49], [35:53]
- The video description quotes different figures for a Phoenix trio, which are not stated in the captions and were not checked.
- Two speakers are former or current team staff and ESPN data staff, and their coaching anecdotes are their own.

## Q&A

- Diminishing returns over more seasons? Yes, marginal gains decline and the ceiling cannot be found. [19:31]
- Coaching implications (shorter rotations, small-sided practice)? Needs practice data teams hold. [20:32]
- Team effects and plug-and-play players? Open, and noise is large. [21:33]
- Big-to-big versus other pass types? Not analyzed. [22:34]
- What counts as a pass? Any pass that became a shot, with catch-and-shoot stronger. [23:35], [24:07]
- Pairs with unusual improvement? Hard to say, noise is large. [24:37]
- Lead initiators or pick-and-roll players? Bigger samples make it possible. [26:40]
- Star versus role players? Shot clock is in the model, could add a role label. [28:12]
- Worse before better? Not examined. [29:13]
- Beyond catch-and-shoot or lineups? Chemistry defined narrowly, lineup work needs care. [30:45]
- Injury breaks and decay? Not modeled. [33:19]
- Shot frequency and adaptation? Not counted. [34:19]
- Rookies? All players included, no adjustments. [35:23]
- Interaction terms? Slight, significant, not dramatic. [37:59]
- Trades for pairs? No. [39:02]
- Off-ball screens versus better passes? Accuracy cannot be split with current data. [40:33]
- Learning to learn, journeymen and age? Could be added as a classification. [41:33], [43:05]

=== FILE: videos/2025-03-18_pcp9h_M6Ir8_causal-impact-of-offensive-linemen-on-pass-plays/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: pcp9h_M6Ir8
title: "SSAC25: Causal Impact of Offensive Linemen on Pass Plays"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ben Jenkins]
topics: [american-football]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Ben Jenkins of Sumer Sports (also a PhD student at Florida Atlantic University) presents CLIP, a method that applies causal inference to offensive line pass protection using NFL tracking data. He argues that player credit is usually estimated as a residual from a prediction model, which relies on correlation. His alternative uses a doubly robust estimator with an outcome model and a propensity model to estimate, per lineman and per tenth of a second, the effect of allowing pressure on completion probability. He reports validation against honors, salary ranking and Pro Football Focus, plus robustness checks, and a short Q&A on features and college use.

## Key claims

- To the speaker's knowledge this is the first public use of causal inference on the offensive line and one of the few on NFL tracking data. [00:00], [00:30]
- Player performance is a causal problem often treated as prediction. Metrics such as rush yards over expected use a residual from a predicted value and rely on correlation. [00:30], [01:00]
- CLIP estimates how pressure allowed by offensive linemen affects completion probability. [01:30], [02:00]
- Machine learning predicts what is likely, and causal inference seeks why and how. [02:31]
- The estimator is doubly robust, needing only one of its two models to be correctly specified. [03:01]
- The target is a conditional average treatment effect per player per play. [03:31]
- On a failed-block play the model flagged the two linemen who failed, and values update every tenth of a second. [04:01], [04:31], [05:01]
- On a clean-protection play, every lineman contributed positively, and the line as a whole was credited with a larger share. [05:31], [06:01]
- The causal model identified All-Pro and Pro Bowl linemen better than other techniques and ranked players by salary more consistently. [06:33]
- On a 2023 Big Data Bowl sample the model correlated strongly with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences the speaker attributes to PFF having the entire data set. [07:03]
- The model correlates with play-level completion percentage, and the speaker says teams with better lines complete more and win more. [07:34]
- The method could extend to other positions and to basketball, soccer or hockey. [09:05], [09:35]
- Q&A: the two models are separate, and inverse propensity weighting creates a balanced data set. [10:35]
- Q&A: the college level has computer vision tracking data, so the method can apply, with extra account of competition quality. [12:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- Example of a residual metric: expected 4 yards, ran 26, residual 22 yards (caption name "Damen Harris"). [02:00]
- CATE: expected completion given pressure minus expected completion given no pressure, per player per play. [03:31]
- Failed-block play: line value 0.10 to 0.15, described as 10 to 15% of the completion attributable to the line. Captions read "start at01 to 0.15" (garbled). [05:01]
- Clean-protection play: line value 0.6 to 0.8, described as 60 to 80%. Captions read "6 to8." [06:01]
- Sample: Big Data Bowl 2023 data, first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 NFL season. [07:03]
- Covariate balance: standardized mean differences under 0.1 after weighting. [08:05]
- Sensitivity: less than 3% variation in CATE values across simulated unobserved confounders. [08:35]
- Time resolution: every tenth of a second. [04:31]
- Pressure is a binary variable, modeled as a probability from zero to one. [13:35]
- The acronym: causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays (captions vary between "alignment" and "lineman"). [01:30]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Doubly robust estimator: an outcome model (completion probability from features and pressure allowed) plus a propensity score model (probability the lineman allows pressure). [03:01]
- Inverse propensity weighting. [10:35]
- Validation: honors, salary rank, PFF comparison, covariate balance, placebo test, random subset consistency, sensitivity to unobserved confounding, calibration and AUC curves. [06:33], [08:05], [08:35]
- Features (Q&A): tracking data for all offensive, defensive and other players, proximity to the quarterback and to the nearest defenders, speed and distance to quarterback. [11:35]

## Limits and open questions

- The method is the speaker's, and he works at Sumer Sports (commercial and institutional view).
- Public sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. No play counts, player counts or confidence intervals are given.
- The attributed line share differs widely between the two example plays (10 to 15% versus 60 to 80%), and the talk does not explain the difference.
- Validation uses honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not measures of cause (Inference).
- The speaker said feature handling was left to the model to work out, and one questioner found the features confusing. [11:05], [11:35]
- College use needs competition-quality adjustment, which was not shown. [12:35]

## Q&A

- Is it propensity to allow pressure times its effect on completion? Yes, in simple terms. [10:05]
- Is pressure an input? No, two separate models. [10:35]
- What are the features? Tracking data including all linemen, teammates and opponents. [11:05], [11:35]
- Does it apply to college, including non-Power-4 schools? Yes with college tracking data and a competition adjustment. [12:05], [12:35]
- Is treatment binary? Yes, but modeled as a probability. [13:05], [13:35]

type: video-summary

## Summary

Three executives from basketball, football and baseball, with an ESPN moderator, discuss how they got their jobs and how they decide under public scrutiny. The recurring argument is that conviction and a sound process matter more than results of any single move, since results are noisy and much of the draft is a coin flip. They describe trades and signings (a first-round trade up, a late-round pick for a released receiver, a record free-agent signing), a risk view based on outcome distributions, limits on AI in play calling, college revenue sharing, and treating players honestly. It is a conversation with no data shown.
